title: Door-to-needle time for stroke thrombolysis at a regional primary stroke centre
subtitle: Process mapping and PDSA cycles with case-by-case run charts
statement: The regional primary stroke centre thrombolysed 94 patients in 2025 with a median door-to-needle time of 62 minutes; only 27 percent were treated within the network's 45-minute target. Every case is timed, but the team does not know which steps between pre-alert and needle consume the time, especially at night and weekends. The project will map the pathway with all involved staff and test changes in PDSA cycles over six months.
whoAffected: Patients with acute ischaemic stroke in a mostly rural catchment, paramedics, emergency nurses, CT radiographers, the stroke team, pharmacy, and trauma patients who share the CT scanner.
whatHurts: Every minute of delay to thrombolysis costs brain tissue and lowers the chance of independent recovery. Staff describe frustration with repeated paging and waits for CT.
currentPractice: Pre-alert by paramedics, triage in the emergency department, then CT; the stroke team is paged by three separate calls; the thrombolytic is prepared after the treatment decision; the registrar comes in from home out of hours.
whyNow: A network target that is rarely met, approval from the emergency department and stroke program, and a completed QI screening.
patientCenteredGoal: Every eligible patient receives thrombolysis as fast as safely possible, day or night, without more haemorrhage or treated mimics.
summary: Problem framed as a QI project to shorten door-to-needle time through process mapping and PDSA cycles.
